title: Principal Component Analysis: Directions of Variance
summary: PCA finds orthogonal directions that capture the most variance. Learn why you center first, how the covariance matrix's eigenvectors and the data's SVD give the same components, and how to project, reconstruct and choose how many components to keep.
takeaways: Always center first. A correct PCA gives the same components when you shift the data.
The sample covariance divides by n − 1. Its eigenvectors are the components and its eigenvalues are the variances along them.
np.linalg.eigh returns eigenvalues in ascending order with eigenvectors in columns, so reverse and transpose.
SVD of the centered data gives the same components (rows of Vᵀ) and variances (S²/(n−1)), up to sign. Fix a sign convention.

steps.label: Center
steps.detail: Subtract each feature's mean: Xc = X − mean.

steps.label: Covariance or SVD
steps.detail: Either C = Xcᵀ Xc / (n − 1), or the thin SVD Xc = U S Vᵀ.

steps.label: Sort + sign-fix
steps.detail: Order components by variance, largest first, and make each one's largest entry positive.

steps.label: Choose k
steps.detail: Keep the smallest k whose cumulative explained variance ratio reaches your threshold.

steps.label: Project / reconstruct
steps.detail: Z = Xc Wᵀ, and X̂ = Z W + mean.

terms.definition: A unit vector along which the projected data has maximal variance, orthogonal to all earlier components.
C = Xcᵀ Xc / (n − 1): pairwise co-variation of features. The diagonal holds each feature's variance.
C = V Λ Vᵀ for a symmetric C: orthonormal eigenvectors V and real eigenvalues Λ.
Xc = U S Vᵀ. The right singular vectors are the principal components and S²/(n − 1) the variances.
Each component's variance divided by the total variance, trace(C).
